proposals.observation: Two CI workflows failed in the last 24 hours: "Funnel-Hack Digest" at 20:25 UTC and "Daily Blog Post" at 15:23 UTC. The content queue shows only 1 post queued against 47 published, meaning the pipeline is the only thing standing between Joel and a content drought. With no quiz completions and no new email signups visible in the window, consistent blog output is the primary top-of-funnel activity still in motion. A failed workflow means that post did not go out, and the queue is thin enough that one more failed run produces a gap in publication.
proposals.proposal: Diagnose and patch the "Daily Blog Post" workflow. The run failed at 15:23 UTC on 28 August. Check the Actions log for the exact step that errored (likely an API key expiry, a broken frontmatter schema, or a rate-limit on the LLM call). The fix is almost certainly one of: rotating a secret, correcting an environment variable reference, or adding a retry block to the HTTP step. Because .github/workflows/* is on the blocked-paths list, the actual workflow file cannot be edited here, but the most common fix lives one level up: the secret or the content-generation script it calls. If the failure is in the generation script, that file is in-bounds. Check the workflow log, identify the failing step name, and patch the script it invokes. The specific change below assumes the most common failure mode: the OpenAI API key secret name was renamed and the script still references the old name.

proposals.impact: capitalises on 66.67% open rate with stronger second-touch
proposals.observation: The Money Vigilance automation has a 66.67% open rate across 12 sends, the strongest of the three active sequences. Money Avoidance is at 52.63% and Money Worship sits at 37.5%. The Vigilance audience is clearly engaged at the subject-line level, but open rate alone does not move people to book a call or reply. If email two in that sequence lands flat, or if it uses generic personal-finance reassurance language, Joel is leaving the most warmed-up segment of his list without a compelling reason to take a next step.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the opening of the second email in the Money Vigilance sequence to match the specific internal experience of a vigilant money personality rather than describing it from the outside. Vigilant earners do not feel chaotic around money. They feel controlled and slightly ashamed of how controlled they feel. The current opening (see CURRENT_TEXT) names the behaviour but stays at the level of a Wikipedia summary. The replacement roots it in a recognisable physical moment, passes the Sultanic test, and gives a clear next step without a false pivot.
proposals.current_text:
Money Vigilance means you take your finances seriously. You're careful, you plan ahead, and you rarely make impulsive decisions. That's genuinely a strength — but it can also mean you hold back even when moving forward would serve you better.

If that sounds familiar, you're in the right place.
proposals.new_text:
You probably checked your bank balance this morning before you checked your messages. Not because anything was wrong. Just because not checking feels irresponsible.

That habit has kept you solvent through things that broke other people's finances. It has also meant you sit on decisions for months that most people would make in an afternoon, and you feel faintly suspicious of anyone who tells you to loosen up about money.

Joel works specifically with people who are careful in a way that has started to cost them. If that sentence produced a quiet recognition rather than defensiveness, reply to this email with one word: yes. That is the only next step.

proposals.impact: converts the one intro-load session that did not proceed
proposals.observation: The quiz recorded one session in 48 hours. That session loaded the intro page and stopped. Completion rate is 0%. The source was direct traffic, meaning someone typed the URL or clicked a saved link rather than arriving cold. That person had enough intent to seek the quiz out. They stopped at the first screen. The intro screen is therefore the single highest-friction point in the funnel right now, and it is the only lever available without quiz-infrastructure changes.
proposals.proposal: Add a one-sentence orientation line to the quiz intro that names what the person is about to do and approximately how long it takes. Right now the intro loads without telling the visitor why this quiz is different from a generic money personality test or how much of their time it will cost. A direct-traffic visitor who already knows the brand still needs a reason to commit the next three minutes. The change is purely additive: one line inserted below the existing heading, before the start button.
proposals.current_text: <start-button label or sub-heading that sits immediately above the CTA — insert the new line before this element>
proposals.new_text: This takes about three minutes. It identifies the specific pattern underneath your money decisions — not a broad type, but the thing that keeps showing up in your own finances. Joel built it from twelve years of one-to-one client work, including his own reckoning with a gym bag full of unopened post and a tax return he had not filed in two years.
